question: Is the mind one abiding thing with many objects, or only momentary cognitions each fixed to one object? (YBh 1.32)

sides.position: Vyāsa: the mind is one, has many objects and abides; otherwise every mind would be one-pointed, no mind distracted; memory, the enjoyer of the karma-store, and the single notion 'I' would be unaccountable.

The unnamed opponent in the bhāṣya: the mind is only a cognition fixed to each object (pratyartha-niyata) and momentary; the one-pointedness of a stream of like cognitions belongs to the stream or to its parts. Vyāsa does not name the opponent.

candidate_readings: a dispute about the nature of mind stated inside one text; other traditions' own texts are needed for the opponent's side

question: Is there a real whole (avayavin) over and above the aggregation of atoms? (YBh 1.43)

sides.position: Vyāsa: the whole exists — one, great or small, touchable, active, impermanent; ordinary dealings are carried out with it; it is the object of nirvitarkā coalescence; otherwise almost all cognition would be false and even right knowledge would have no object.
The unnamed opponent: the aggregation of atoms is not a real thing (avastuka) and the subtle cause is imperceptible, so there is no whole.

question: What is the 'non-seeing' (adarśana) that is the occasion of the conjunction of seer and seen? (YBh 2.23)

sides.position: Views listed by Vyāsa as found in the śāstra: the office of the guṇas; the non-arising of the pradhāna-mind for the seer to whom objects are shown; the absence of seeing while the seen exists; ignorance stilled with its mind as seed of the mind's arising; the manifestation of the impression of motion on the exhaustion of that of stillness.
Others in the śāstra: seeing-power itself is non-seeing; non-seeing is a property of both; knowledge itself is non-seeing.

question: Is liberation only the cessation of the mind? (YBh 2.24)

sides.position: The 'partial teacher' (ācāryadeśīya): with the cause of non-seeing absent the buddhi ceases; liberation is the cessation of the mind.
The objector's tale of the impotent husband: knowledge that exists does not bring cessation of the mind; what hope that it will after it is destroyed? Vyāsa's own reply is not in this segment.

question: What is mastery of the senses (indriya-jaya)? (YBh 2.55)

sides.position: Non-addiction to sound and other objects (attachment is addiction, since it throws one off the better).
Contact with sound and the rest at one's own wish; or knowledge of them empty of pleasure and pain when attachment and aversion are absent.

Jaigīṣavya: non-engagement (apratipatti) through one-pointedness of mind; Vyāsa adds that the mastery following sense-withdrawal is supreme because the senses, stilled with the mind, need no other effort-made means.
